lessons.title: Lesson 1: What NCCER Core is and how credentials are earned
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what NCCER Core covers and how a learner earns an NCCER credential.
This lesson builds toward: Using the NCCER website and your own calendar, you will write a training-and-test plan for NCCER Core with a center, modules and dates, with a real center or program, every Core module listed and a target test date.
NCCER is the National Center for Construction Education and Research. It writes training for construction crafts and keeps a record of the credentials people earn. Core is the starting curriculum that most crafts build on.
In the Core 6th edition, the modules are: Basic Safety (Construction Site Safety Orientation), Introduction to Construction Math, Introduction to Hand Tools, Introduction to Power Tools, Introduction to Construction Drawings, Basic Communication Skills, Basic Employability Skills and Introduction to Materials Handling. Build Your Future in Construction and Introduction to Basic Rigging are electives. Check the Core page, because editions change.
NCCER credentials are earned at accredited training locations. You take written tests on what you know, and you perform tasks safely while an evaluator watches. Your results are tracked under your own NCCER number so employers can check them online.
Core is often taught in high schools, community colleges, job and re-entry programs and pre-apprenticeships. Use NCCER's Find a Center page to look for one near you. This course gets you ready; it does not give you the credential.
Step by step:
- Open nccer.org and find the Core page in the craft catalog.
- Write down the Core modules for the current edition.
- Open the Find a Center page and search near you.
- Write down two places near you and how to contact them.
Words to know:
- NCCER: National Center for Construction Education and Research: the group that writes this construction training and tracks credentials.
- Core: the first NCCER curriculum; most construction crafts start with it.
- Module: one unit of a curriculum, like one chapter of a book, with its own test.
- Credential: proof that you passed training and tests, which an employer can check.
- Accredited: approved by NCCER to train and test learners for NCCER credentials.
- Pre-apprenticeship: a short program that prepares you to get into an apprenticeship.
Official sources:
- NCCER: Core curriculum (craft catalog)
- NCCER: Industry-recognized credentials
- NCCER: Find a Center
- Apprenticeship.gov: What is a pre-apprenticeship?
Try it now: Open the NCCER Core page and the Find a Center page. On paper, write the Core modules and the names of two places near you that teach or test NCCER. If you cannot get online, write the modules from this lesson and ask your local American Job Center which programs teach NCCER Core.
You can now say what NCCER Core covers, how its credentials are earned, and where to look for a program near you.

check.why: NCCER credentials come from accredited locations, with written tests and hands-on tasks.

check.q: What does this Koach Learn course do?
options: Prepares you for Core training and testing
check.why: It prepares you; the credential comes from an accredited program.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Job-site safety: the Focus Four and their controls
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the Focus Four hazards on a job site and name a control for each.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job-site scene or a list of tasks, you will identify the Focus Four hazards and name a control for each one, getting at least 4 of 5 right, including the 6-foot fall protection rule and the ladder rules.
OSHA calls the four biggest killers in construction the Focus Four: falls, struck-by, caught-in or -between, and electrocution. Basic Safety in Core starts here.
Falls: OSHA requires fall protection at six feet or more in construction, such as guardrails, safety nets or a personal fall arrest system. Cover or guard holes. On a portable ladder used to reach an upper level, the side rails must go at least 3 feet above the landing, and the foot sits about one foot out for every four feet of height (the 4-to-1 rule).
Struck-by: wear a hard hat and high-visibility vest, stay out from under loads, and never stand behind a backing vehicle. Caught-in or -between: stay out of unprotected trenches and keep away from moving parts and swinging equipment. Electrocution: look up for power lines, use tools on GFCI-protected outlets, and never work on live circuits unless you are trained and authorized.
PPE is the last line of defense. Safety glasses, hard hat, gloves, hearing protection and boots protect you, but removing or guarding the hazard comes first. If something looks unsafe, stop and tell your supervisor.
Step by step:
- Look at the task and the area around it.
- Ask: can someone fall, be hit, be caught, or touch electricity?
- Name the control: guard, cover, distance, protection or shutting off power.
- Put on the right PPE.
- If you cannot control it, stop and tell your supervisor.
Words to know:
- Focus Four: OSHA's name for the four leading causes of construction deaths: falls, struck-by, caught-in or -between, and electrocution.
- Fall protection: guardrails, safety nets or a harness system that stop or prevent a fall.
- GFCI: ground-fault circuit interrupter: a device that cuts power fast when current leaks, to prevent shock.
- PPE: personal protective equipment: hard hat, safety glasses, gloves, boots, hearing protection, vest.
- Control: a way to remove or reduce a hazard.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Construction Focus Four training
- OSHA: Fall protection
- OSHA: 29 CFR 1926.1053, Ladders
Try it now: Draw a simple job site on paper: a two-story house frame, a ladder, a trench, a power line and a truck. Mark one Focus Four hazard for each and write the control next to it. Then work out how far out the foot of a ladder should be if it reaches 16 feet up (answer: about 4 feet).
You can now name the Focus Four hazards, give a control for each, and use the 6-foot and ladder rules.

check.q: A worker is on a roof edge 10 feet up with no guardrail. What applies?
options: Only a hard hat is needed
Fall protection is needed at 6 feet or more
check.why: OSHA requires fall protection at six feet or more in construction.

check.q: A ladder reaches 12 feet up a wall. About how far out should its foot be?
check.why: The 4-to-1 rule: 1 foot out for every 4 feet up, so 12 / 4 = 3 feet.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Construction math: the tape measure and fractions
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read a tape measure to the nearest 1/16 inch and add and convert feet and inches.
This lesson builds toward: Using a tape measure or a drawing of one, and paper, you will read measurements to the nearest 1/16 inch and add, subtract and convert feet and inches, with at least 4 of 5 answers exactly right.
Most tape measures in US construction mark each inch in sixteenths. The longest line in the middle of an inch is 1/2. The next shorter lines are 1/4 and 3/4, then the eighths, then the shortest lines are sixteenths. Count the small lines past the last whole inch: 6 small lines past 5 inches is 5 6/16, which reduces to 5 3/8.
To reduce, divide the top and bottom by 2 until the top is odd: 12/16 = 6/8 = 3/4. To add fractions, give them the same bottom number: 2 3/4 + 1 5/8 = 2 6/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 11/8 = 4 3/8.
One foot is 12 inches. To change feet to inches, multiply by 12 and add the extra inches: 7 feet 4 inches = 84 + 4 = 88 inches. To change inches to feet, divide by 12; the remainder is inches: 100 inches = 8 feet 4 inches.
Check square with the 3-4-5 rule: measure 3 feet along one side and 4 feet along the other; if the diagonal between those marks is 5 feet, the corner is square. Measure twice, cut once.
Step by step:
- Find the last whole inch before the end of what you measure.
- Count the sixteenth lines past it.
- Write the number as sixteenths, then reduce.
- For feet and inches, multiply feet by 12 and add the inches.
- Check your answer by measuring again.
Words to know:
- Sixteenth: 1/16 of an inch, the smallest mark on most construction tape measures.
- Reduce: write a fraction with smaller numbers that mean the same, like 8/16 = 1/2.
- Square: a corner of exactly 90 degrees.
- 3-4-5 rule: a way to check a corner is square: 3 and 4 along the sides make 5 on the diagonal.
Try it now: On paper, solve: (1) 9 feet 7 inches in inches; (2) 3 7/16 + 2 5/8; (3) 50 inches in feet and inches; (4) 10/16 reduced. Answers: 115 inches; 6 1/16; 4 feet 2 inches; 5/8. If you have a tape measure, measure a table, a door and a book to the nearest 1/16 inch.
You can now read a tape measure to 1/16 inch, reduce and add fractions, convert feet and inches, and check a corner for square.

check.q: What is 6 feet 3 inches in inches?

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Hand and power tools: choose, check and use safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a suitable tool for a task and list the safety checks before using it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a cutting, drilling or fastening task, you will choose a suitable hand or power tool and list the safety checks to make before using it, naming at least three correct checks, including guards, cord and power off when changing a blade or bit.
Pick the tool made for the job. A claw hammer drives and pulls nails; a tape measure, speed square and level mark and check; a handsaw or circular saw cuts boards; a drill drives screws and makes holes; a utility knife scores drywall. Using the wrong tool, like a screwdriver as a chisel, causes injuries and damage.
Before you use any tool, inspect it. Hand tools: no loose heads, cracked handles or mushroomed striking faces. Power tools: guards in place and working, cord and plug with no cuts or missing ground pin, switch works, blade or bit sharp and the right type.
When you change a blade or bit, unplug the tool or take the battery out. Never carry a tool by its cord or yank the cord out. Keep cords out of walkways. Wear safety glasses every time, and hearing protection with loud tools.
Tool use is a hands-on skill. Learn and practice each power tool with an instructor before you use it on your own, and follow the maker's manual and your site's rules.
Step by step:
- Choose the tool made for the task.
- Inspect it: handle, head, guard, cord, plug, switch, blade or bit.
- Put on safety glasses and other PPE.
- Unplug or remove the battery before changing a blade or bit.
- Tag and report a damaged tool; do not use it.
Words to know:
- Guard: a cover on a power tool that keeps your hands away from the blade or moving parts.
- Ground pin: the round third prong on a plug that helps prevent shock.
- Speed square: a triangle-shaped tool for marking straight and angled lines.
- Mushroomed: when the striking end of a chisel or punch spreads out from being hit; pieces can fly off.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Hand and power tools
Try it now: For each task, write the tool and three checks you would make: (1) cut a 2x4 to length; (2) drive screws into a deck board; (3) pull a bent nail. Example for (1): circular saw; guard closes on its own, cord and plug undamaged, blade sharp and tight.
You can now choose a tool for a task, inspect it, and follow the safe habits for hand and power tools.

check.q: You need to change the blade on a circular saw. What do you do first?
options: Ask a coworker to hold it running
check.why: Unplugging, or taking the battery out, stops the saw from starting while your hands are on the blade.

check.q: The plug on an extension cord is missing its ground pin. What do you do?
options: Take it out of use and report it
check.why: A damaged plug is a shock hazard; tag it out and report it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading construction drawings and making a cut list
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the title block, scale, views and dimensions on a drawing and write a cut list from it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple construction drawing, you will find the title block, scale, views and dimensions and turn them into a cut list, with every length correct to the nearest 1/16 inch. Using a tape measure or a drawing of one, and paper, you will read measurements to the nearest 1/16 inch and add, subtract and convert feet and inches, with at least 4 of 5 answers exactly right.
Construction drawings, also called plans or blueprints, show what to build. Start with the title block: the project name, sheet number, date, who drew it and the scale. The legend explains the symbols and abbreviations.
Drawings show different views. A plan view looks down from above. An elevation looks straight at one side. A section is a slice through the building that shows the inside. A detail is a close-up of one part.
The scale tells you how the drawing relates to real size. At 1/4 inch = 1 foot, a line 2 1/2 inches long is 10 feet. Always use the written dimensions; if a written dimension is missing or does not fit, ask your supervisor instead of measuring the paper.
A cut list turns a drawing into pieces to cut: name, how many, length. For a frame 36 inches wide and 24 inches tall made of 3/4 inch boards, with the side pieces fitted between the top and bottom: top and bottom are 2 at 36 inches; the sides are 2 at 24 - 3/4 - 3/4 = 22 1/2 inches.
Step by step:
- Read the title block: project, sheet, date and scale.
- Read the legend for symbols.
- Find the view you need: plan, elevation, section or detail.
- Write the dimensions for each part.
- Subtract for parts that overlap, then write the cut list: piece, how many, length.
Words to know:
- Title block: the box on a drawing with the project name, sheet number, date and scale.
- Scale: how the drawing size relates to real size, like 1/4 inch = 1 foot.
- Plan view: a drawing looking down from above.
- Elevation: a drawing looking straight at one side.
- Cut list: a list of pieces to cut, with how many and how long.
Try it now: Draw a box on paper and label it 48 inches wide and 30 inches tall, made of 3/4 inch boards, with the sides fitted between the top and bottom. Write the cut list. Answer: 2 at 48 inches and 2 at 28 1/2 inches. Then: at 1/4 inch = 1 foot, how long is a wall drawn 3 3/4 inches long? (Answer: 15 feet.)
You can now read the title block, scale and views of a simple drawing and turn its dimensions into a cut list.

check.q: Where do you find the scale and sheet number on a drawing?
options: On the back of the sheet
In the legend of symbols only
check.why: The title block holds the project name, sheet number, date and scale.

check.q: The scale is 1/4 inch = 1 foot. A wall is drawn 2 inches long. How long is it?
check.why: 2 inches is eight quarter inches, so 8 feet.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Materials handling, teamwork and your Core plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a safe lift and carry of materials and write a dated training-and-test plan for NCCER Core.
This lesson builds toward: Given a load of materials to move or store, you will plan a safe lift, carry and stack, including when to get help or equipment, covering the weight check, path, lifting posture and stacking. Using the NCCER website and your own calendar, you will write a training-and-test plan for NCCER Core with a center, modules and dates, with a real center or program, every Core module listed and a target test date.
Before you lift, size up the load: how heavy, how big, any sharp edges. Check your path for trips and doorways. If it is heavy or awkward, get a coworker or use a cart, dolly or other equipment you are trained on. Lift with your legs: feet apart, bend your knees, keep the load close, do not twist. Turn with your feet.
Stack materials on flat, solid ground, heavy items low, and use blocking or cross-stacking so piles do not slide or roll. Keep walkways and exits clear. Carry long boards with the front end high and watch the back end when you turn.
Good crew members show up on time, ready, with their PPE. They listen, repeat instructions back ("Cut four at 22 and a half, got it"), ask when unsure, and report hazards right away. Core teaches these as Basic Communication and Basic Employability Skills.
Now make your plan. Choose a center or program, list the Core modules, pick a start date and a weekly study time, and set a target date for your tests. Put the dates in your calendar and tell someone who will check on you.
Step by step:
- Size up the load and the path.
- Get help or equipment for heavy or awkward loads.
- Lift with your legs, keep it close, do not twist.
- Stack on solid ground, heavy low, walkways clear.
- Write your plan: center, modules, start date, weekly time, test date.
Words to know:
- Blocking: pieces of wood placed to keep a pile from rolling or sliding.
- Cross-stacking: laying each layer across the one below so the pile stays steady.
- Repeat back: saying an instruction back to the person who gave it, so both know it was heard right.
Official sources:
- NCCER: Find a Center
- NCCER: Core curriculum (craft catalog)
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
Try it now: Write a lift plan for moving ten 12-foot 2x6 boards from a truck to a work area 50 feet away: the weight check, the path, who helps, how you carry, and how you stack. Then start your Core plan: write the center you found in Lesson 1, the Core modules, a start date, your weekly study time and a target test date.
You can now plan a safe lift, carry and stack, act as a good crew member, and write a dated plan to train and test for NCCER Core.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Cut list Lengths are missing or ignore the 3/4 inch boards. Two pieces at 36 inches and two at 22 1/2 inches, with piece names and counts. Also notes saw kerf and marks which face to measure from. Measuring and math Fractions are wrong or not reduced. Every length is correct to the nearest 1/16 inch and reduced. Shows the math and checks the frame for square with the 3-4-5 rule. Tool choice and checks No tool named, or fewer than three checks. Names a suitable saw and three correct checks, including guard, cord and unplugging to change the blade. Also lists PPE and says the tool will be used only after instructor training. Safe handling No plan for weight, path or stacking. Covers weight check, path, lifting posture and stacking. Also says when to get a helper or equipment and how to carry long boards through turns. Site hazards No hazards named. Names at least two Focus Four hazards that could apply and a control for each. Covers all four with controls. Training-and-test plan No center or no dates. A real center or program, the Core modules, a start date, weekly study time and a target test date. Dates are in a calendar and a support person is named. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A box is heavier than you can lift comfortably. What do you do?
options: Lift it fast to get it over with
Get a coworker or use a cart
check.why: Heavy or awkward loads need help or equipment.

options: "Center: county job program; Core modules; start Nov 3; Tue and Thu 6-8 pm; target test Feb 15."
check.why: It names a center, the modules, a start date, weekly time and a target test date.
